title: How Project Star Gate Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Project Stargate, the US government's program (roughly 1972 to 1995) to study and use remote viewing and other psychic abilities for intelligence gathering. They cover its Cold War origins (Soviet TV demonstrations by Nina Kulagina, fears of a Soviet mind weapon), early funding of SRI International and Russell Targ, Uri Geller's influence on Jimmy Carter, the Army's Project Grill Flame at Fort Meade, Joseph McMonagle's anecdotes, Edwin May's stricter forced-choice protocols and ranked-order judging, famous claimed hits (West Virginia site, Ural site, microwave generator, gantry crane, Angela Ford's Charles Jordan find), and why the CIA ultimately abandoned it after an American Institutes for Research evaluation said it was not usable for intelligence. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about heroin addiction in Kensington, Philadelphia, and a plug for a book and the show's company.

segments.title: Book promo and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts promote their upcoming book, greet listeners, and tease Project Stargate, joking about its questionable reality and mentioning the John Ronson book and film.

segments.title: Origins: Soviet psychic fears and the Cold War arms race
segments.summary: The hosts describe how a Soviet TV demonstration of telekinesis by Nina Kulagina alarmed US defense analysts, prompting a US effort to match Soviet psychic research. They define remote viewing and anomalous cognition as extrasensory perception.

segments.title: SRI, Russell Targ, and early remote viewing sessions
segments.summary: DIA and CIA begin funding private research at SRI in California in 1972 and 1973. Russell Targ's 1976 Washington Square Park experiment is described, and Uri Geller's talk with President-elect Jimmy Carter is recounted as a factor in continued interest.

segments.title: Project Grill Flame and the Army's barracks testing
segments.summary: The Army took over under the name Project Grill Flame at Fort Meade, Maryland, where remote viewers were given envelopes with coordinates or photos and recorded impressions that analysts then reviewed.

segments.title: Joseph McMonagle's claimed hits and skepticism
segments.summary: Joseph McMonagle's anecdotal claims are discussed, including predicting Skylab's crash and a hostage tip about Brigadier General James Dozier, plus a KGB agent calculator story. The hosts note that they could not corroborate these with declassified documents.

segments.title: CIA handoffs, renaming to Stargate, and declassification
segments.summary: The program moved between agencies and contractors, was renamed Stargate around 1990, was defunded by the CIA, and its records were declassified about five years later. The hosts discuss skeptic Brian Dunning's view of this.

segments.title: Edwin May, forced-choice testing, and ranked order judging
segments.summary: Edwin May, a nuclear physicist who took over, introduced stricter protocols including forced-choice testing with ranked order judging using National Geographic photos. The hosts explain the procedure and its statistical weaknesses, including subjective judging and reused images.

segments.title: Famous claimed hits and the AIR evaluation
segments.summary: Claimed successes are described: a West Virginia underground site, a Ural Mountains site, a microwave generator report, a Russian gantry crane drawing, and Angela Ford's remote viewing that located Charles Jordan. The American Institutes for Research evaluation found the results not usable for intelligence, and the program was shut down after about twenty years and roughly twenty million dollars.

segments.title: Wrap-up and mail teaser
segments.summary: Hosts summarize why intelligence analysts found the output unhelpful, mention the Mars remote viewing transcript as further reading, and transition to listener mail.
